clue.text: Figure of speech to hamper eccentric

indicators.note: something eccentric is odd and out of line, so the preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words supply the fodder letter for letter

explanation.surface: A figure of speech is called on to hold back some oddball.
explanation.definitionFit: A metaphor is a standard example of a rhetorical device, describing one thing in terms of another.

clue.text: Evil intent of nursemaid following male

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the nursemaid is placed behind the other piece

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
Alice is the nursemaid in A. A. Milne's poem about Buckingham Palace

explanation.surface: A nanny walking behind a man has sinister plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts the nursemaid after the male. In Milne's verse Christopher Robin went down with Alice to see the guard changed.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is the desire to harm others, which is precisely evil intent.

clue.text: Local in group turning up for game

indicators.note: in places one word inside another
in a down clue, turning up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: a set is a group
a local is a pub near home

explanation.surface: Friends from the pub turn out for a match.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is British for one's neighbourhood pub; it sits inside S_ET before the whole is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is a racket sport, an example of a game.

clue.text: Safeguard for London theatre

blocks.note: first meaning: a protection, after the statue of Pallas that guarded Troy
second meaning: the famous variety theatre in the West End

explanation.surface: A security measure for a West End playhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a protecting safeguard, from the Trojan statue of Pallas, and names a large West End variety house.

clue.text: Practised and made a cocktail

blocks.note: old as in an old hand, experienced
fashioned means made or shaped

explanation.surface: Someone rehearsed and then mixed a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An Old Fashioned is a classic whisky drink with bitters and sugar, a named cocktail.

clue.text: Cruel, removing tail from bird

indicators.note: taking away the tail means the final letter of the bird is dropped

blocks.note: a bittern is a wading bird of the heron family

explanation.surface: Someone is being cruel by pulling the tail feathers off a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter wind or bitter remark is harsh and painful, a synonym of cruel.

clue.text: Country of vermouth nearly all year?

indicators.note: nearly means the word stops one letter short of its end

blocks.note: it is Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
the word shorn of its last letter
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A nation where vermouth flows almost all year round.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and it is a British bar order: gin with Italian vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Italy is a European country, and also the home of vermouth.

clue.text: Old aircraft's flight over country road

blocks.note: a trip is a flight, a journey
a lane is a narrow country road

explanation.surface: A vintage plane flies over a rural road.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, over puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A triplane, with three stacked wings, is an early type of aeroplane from the First World War era.

clue.text: People at it are close to fighting

definitions.text: People at it are close to fighting

blocks.clueFragment: People at it are close to fighting
blocks.note: surface reading: people about to start a brawl
setter's reading: physically near a boxing match, in the front seats

explanation.walkthrough: Close to fighting suggests tempers fraying, but it means seated next to the boxing ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringside is the area immediately beside a boxing ring, where spectators are nearest the bout.

clue.text: Woman on ground who is in charge of the diggings?

definitions.text: who is in charge of the diggings
definitions.note: read as 'one who is in charge of the diggings'

blocks.note: ground is land
a lady is a woman

explanation.surface: A woman stands on the ground supervising an excavation, like an archaeologist on site.
explanation.walkthrough: Diggings, or digs, is British slang for rented lodgings, not an excavation.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlady runs the lodgings where tenants rent rooms, so she is the person who manages the digs.

clue.text: Putting name on correspondence is helping

indicators.note: putting one thing on another sets it after, so the order of the pieces is fixed by these words
in an across clue, on means placed after, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: a ratio is a correspondence between two quantities
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Adding a name to letters is a help.
explanation.walkthrough: Correspondence suggests letters, but here it means a proportional relation.
explanation.definitionFit: A helping is one portion of food, and a ration is a fixed portion allotted to each person.

clue.text: Patch actor is suffering, as in denouement of tragedy

indicators.note: suffering means being knocked about, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: the fodder letter for letter
joins the fodder too

explanation.surface: A stopgap actor is struggling, as at the end of a tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The catastrophe is the final turn of a classical tragedy, so something like it is disastrous.

clue.text: What's tea put round in?

indicators.note: put round means one word is wrapped about another

blocks.note: cha is a slang word for tea
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what tea is served in when it goes round.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: tea is poured into cups made of fine porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: China is the porcelain teacups and pots are made from, so tea is served in it.

clue.text: Everyone is embracing contrary girl, a native of South Africa

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so one part goes inside the others

blocks.note: everyone is all, followed by is
the nursery rhyme begins 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary'

explanation.surface: A whole group hugs a stubborn girl who comes from South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrary' looks like a reversal signal, but it points to the nursery-rhyme Mary. She goes in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The amaryllis, or belladonna lily, is a flowering bulb that grows wild in the Cape region.

clue.text: Cast down, as when Faust is presented fast?

blocks.clueFragment: as when Faust is presented fast?
blocks.note: surface reading: a production of Goethe's or Gounod's Faust that runs at speed
setter's reading: the name loses its middle letter, its heart, and becomes a different word

explanation.surface: Someone feels gloomy, like an audience watching Faust rushed through.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of FAUST is U; take it away and FAST is left, so the word has been dis-heartened.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cast down is to be dejected, which is the everyday meaning of having lost heart.

clue.text: One who sniggers about wife is a nervous type

indicators.note: about means going round the other piece

blocks.note: one who titters, giggles
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A man who smirks at his wife is a jittery sort.
explanation.definitionFit: To twitter is to be in a state of nervous agitation, so a twitterer is a fluttery, anxious person.

clue.text: Coordinate basic reform fool overturned

indicators.note: to reform is to shape anew, so the letters are rearranged
turned over in a down clue means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the fodder as written
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: An instruction to organise a fundamental shake-up after a fool is ousted.
explanation.definitionFit: The abscissa is the x-coordinate of a point, its horizontal distance from the vertical axis.

clue.text: Last users of rubbish

blocks.note: first meaning: shoemakers, who use a last, a foot-shaped block
second meaning: nonsense, in British slang

explanation.surface: The final people to use the junk.
explanation.walkthrough: Last looks like 'final', but it is the shoemaker's foot-shaped mould. Cobblers is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe repairers work on a last, and the plural is also a mild British word for talk that is rot.

clue.text: Binmen footle about in the capital

indicators.note: moved about means scattered into a fresh order

blocks.note: the two words supply the fodder letter for letter

explanation.surface: Dustmen idle around in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: Binmen are British refuse collectors; to footle is to waste time.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloemfontein is the judicial capital of South Africa and capital of the Free State province.

clue.text: Ridiculing work from eccentric composer about king

indicators.note: about means going round the other piece

blocks.note: Erik Satie, the French composer famed for his oddities
R is short for rex, king

explanation.surface: A mocking piece by an odd composer about a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an anagram signal, but it describes the composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A satire is a work that mocks its target, a piece of writing that ridicules.

clue.text: Unkempt bird with grey wings

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its two ends, so only its outermost letters count

blocks.note: a shag is a seabird of the cormorant family
the two end letters of grey

explanation.surface: A scruffy bird with grey wing feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaggy hair or fur is long and untidy, the same as unkempt.

clue.text: Knight from Barcelona, possibly possessing money?

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible rearrangement of the named place
possessing money means the money must appear inside the result in place of another letter

blocks.note: the city name as written
L stands for the pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A Spanish nobleman from Barcelona is perhaps a wealthy man.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose clue: the city's letters are shuffled with its N swapped for the L of money; it also works as a hint at a Spanish gentleman of means.
explanation.definitionFit: Caballero is Spanish for a knight or gentleman, literally a horseman, so it is a knight from Spain.

clue.text: Carouse, up in this bar

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to revel is to carouse

explanation.surface: Partying, there's a drinking establishment here.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar looks like a pub, but it is a rigid rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A lever is a bar pivoted on a fulcrum and used to shift a load.

clue.text: Refuse treatment at first — foolhardy

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: the opening letter of treatment
rash means reckless, foolhardy

explanation.surface: Turning down medical care at the outset is foolhardy.
explanation.walkthrough: Refuse looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse and trash are both nouns for rubbish that is thrown away.

clue.text: Be inclined to provide space for books

blocks.note: first meaning: to slope gradually
second meaning: to fit a room with shelving

explanation.surface: Someone feels like making room on the shelves for books.
explanation.definitionFit: Land that shelves slopes downward gently, and to shelve a room is to put shelves into it.

clue.text: Tea with fine china? How delightful!

blocks.note: char is a British slang word for tea
Ming porcelain is the classic fine Chinese china

explanation.surface: Someone is served tea in good porcelain and exclaims in pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming! is an exclamation of pleasure, and charming as an adjective means delightful.

clue.text: Drink in the sailor's world

blocks.note: an AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor; with the 's
an orb is a globe, the world

explanation.surface: A sailor's world is drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: To drink in something is to take it in fully, the same as soaking it up.

clue.text: Half pierce, being armoured on the outside? Only just

indicators.note: half asks for only part of the word, here its second three letters
on the outside means wrapping around the other piece

blocks.note: covered in scales like armour plating
the back half of pierce

explanation.surface: Something armoured on the outside can be only half pierced, barely penetrated.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcely and only just both mean barely, by the narrowest margin.
